subject: Burst recovery & latency budgeting — private GPU pool (Acme Logistics)
messages:
From: Alex Singh <alex.singh@acmelogistics.com>
To: Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: infra-team@acmelogistics.com
Date: Mon, 14 Sep 2026 15:12:00 -0400
Subject: Private GPU pool sizing — burst scenarios and latency concerns

Sean —

Thanks again for the demo last week. As we move toward pilots, our infra team asked for concrete sizing guidance for a private VPC deployment. Two things are keeping us up at night: sustained bursts during batch document ingestion (spiky ~3–5min windows every hour) and the 95th/99th latency tail for short chat-like calls (<=200ms target ideally).

Could you send over a short run-through of how Redwood recommends sizing a private GPU pool to meet both throughput and tail latency targets, and any recommended mitigation strategies (warm pools, admission control, KV cache warmup, network egress sizing)? Our security/compliance folks will also need the attachments, but high level is fine to start.

Appreciate it —
Alex
Infra Lead | Acme Logistics

From: Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwoodinference.com>
To: Alex Singh <alex.singh@acmelogistics.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwoodinference.com>, Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Mon, 14 Sep 2026 17:03:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Private GPU pool sizing — burst scenarios and latency concerns

Alex —

High level first pass attached (spreadsheet + short PDF). Key takeaways up front:

- Separate control plane targets from inference capacity: aim to provision baseline GPUs to cover steady-state chat traffic + 50% headroom for short bursts.
- For 3–5 minute hourly spikes, we recommend a two-tier strategy: (1) warm standby instances (idle pre-warmed pods) for <10s cold-starts and (2) an admission policy that permits short-lived burst queueing to avoid tail amplification.
- Network: reserve 1.5x egress headroom for KV/weights fetch during warmup and for checkpoint pulls. Watch for packet bursts — jumbo frames and QoS on your VPC peering helps.

I'll have Karthik and Naomi add a concrete capacity table (GPUs, QPS per GPU, expected p95/p99) and a short runbook for warmup and cache priming. Can you confirm your expected steady-state QPS and the peak burst QPS (per region)? That will let us map to a concrete GPU count and a warm pool sizing recommendation.

Best —
Sean
Director, Customer Engineering
Redwood Inference

Attachments: 20260914-acme-burst-model-v2.xlsx (spreadsheet summary), latency-budgeting-notes.pdf (design notes)
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwoodinference.com>
To: Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwoodinference.com>, Alex Singh <alex.singh@acmelogistics.com>
Cc: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwoodinference.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Tue, 15 Sep 2026 09:12:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Private GPU pool sizing — burst scenarios and latency concerns

Alex / Sean —

Following up with the concrete sizing assumptions (see pasted excerpt from tab "Sizing" in the spreadsheet):

- Model: redwood-open-rlhf-7B (int8 q4_0) — baseline throughput: ~18 tokens/sec per GPU for typical chat prompts (len 64). For short chat (<=64 tokens) we map QPS ~= tokens/sec * average tokens. Empirical: ~120 small chat QPS/GPU.
- Steady-state: you suggested ~600 concurrent chat requests during daytime peak. Conservatively map 600 / 120 = 5 GPUs baseline.
- Burst model: ingestion jobs show 3x spike to ~1800 concurrent for 3–5min windows every hour. For that window, target capacity=1800/120=15 GPUs.
- Warm pool strategy: maintain 20% of peak (3 GPUs) as warm preloaded pods to shave cold-start penalty (warmup from kernel selection, KV cache priming). Use continuous background KV warmers tied to common prefixes.
- Admission & graceful degradation: allow short-lived in-memory queueing (max queue latency 200ms) and implement a fast-fail path to a cheaper fp16 variant if p95>250ms for >30s.

Network recommendations:

- Ensure bilateral MTU/jumbo-frames between inference nodes and your VPC egress; this reduces per-token overhead for large payloads.
- Provision egress to object store at ~1.5x expected peak concurrency (estimate 10–12 Gbps in your cluster during ingestion peaks).
- Enable NIC-level QoS to prioritize RPCs for small chat calls and deprioritize large batch checkpoints.

Operational notes (short runbook lines):

1) Pre-warm after deploy: spin warm pool to target (3 GPUs) and run KV primer for top 20 prompt prefixes.
2) Spike detection: if qps > 85% of baseline for >30s, trigger burst autoscale to add GPUs in 60–90s windows (we recommend coarse-grained steps to avoid oscillation).
3) Fallback: roll to a quantized fp16 variant in the same pool if latency breach persists >45s.

I attached the spreadsheet with the full assumptions and a simple cost delta. If the model/product mix differs (e.g., mixing embeddings batches), we'll need to rerun the numbers.

-Karthik
Senior Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Private GPU pool sizing — burst scenarios and latency concerns

Thanks Karthik — this is helpful and close to what we expected. A couple of follow-ups from our infra team:

- Can you clarify the warm pool start time and the minimum pre-warm concurrency? If we maintain 3 warm GPUs, what is the observed cold-start latency to spin an additional pod from 0 to ready (not just model load but also network connectivity)?
- On the admission queue: 200ms max queue latency seems tight for an ingestion spike; is that a hard requirement or configurable? We might be able to accept slightly higher p95 for chat during ingestion windows but not p99.
- Security asked for an artefact describing how fallback to fp16 is audited (we need a short description for our compliance review).

We can commit to sharing actual daily QPS and a couple of ingestion sample windows so you can tune the sizing numbers.

Best,
Alex

From: Naomi Feldman <naomi_feldman@redwoodinference.com>
To: Alex Singh <alex.singh@acmelogistics.com>, Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwoodinference.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Tue, 15 Sep 2026 11:04:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Private GPU pool sizing — burst scenarios and latency concerns

Alex —

Quick answers and next steps:

- Warm-start time (observed): 45–75s to have a new pod schedule and the model kernels selected; model weights load adds 20–40s depending on local disk throughput. With warm preloads (our recommended flow) additional pre-warmed pods come up to serving in ~10–15s because kernels are already selected and the KV cache primed.
- Queue latency target: the 200ms was a conservative goal driven by low-latency chat SLAs. We can make the admission threshold configurable; suggested default is 200–300ms for p95. For p99 we recommend intervention paths (fallback model or redirect traffic to hosted backup) rather than allowing unbounded queuing.
- Auditing fallback to fp16: we produce an event for every fallback decision with the following fields: timestamp, request_id, reason_code (latency_breach/scale_unavailable), original_model, fallback_model, duration_of_fallback, and circuit_id. Those events are retained in your audit log stream for 90 days (configurable) and can be forwarded to your SIEM via our secure webhook. We'll attach a one-page compliance artefact for your security team.

Action items:
1) Sean: request Alex's sample QPS + 2 ingestion windows (CSV) — after that we'll regenerate the spreadsheet with tuned GPU counts and a recommended autoscale curve.
2) Marissa: prepare the compliance artefact (1-pager) on fallback auditing and retention.
3) Karthik: add a short latency SLA decision table to the spreadsheet (p50/p95/p99 mapping to actions).

Alex, if that works I can schedule a 30-minute follow-up with your infra folks tomorrow morning.

Thanks —
Naomi
Head of Product, Redwood Inference
